newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr unsettled by yen rally,rate whispers.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr unsettled by yen rally,rate whispers.

text.p: The Australian dollar took a step back Tuesday, daunted by a rare advance from the yen and a nagging fear the Reserve Bank may yet cut rates here.
In a choppy session the currency first dipped in the face of European selling, then rallied on talk of samurai-linked buying, only to fade again as the yen staged a rally of its own.

Dealers also found it hard to forget the RBA board was holding its monthly meeting today and while analysts were almost unanimous in not expecting an easing, they had been caught long and wrong before. With that in mind, they looked for the dollar to test support at US$0.7790 and perhaps US$0.7775 later.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar had sagged to US$0.7794/99 from Monday's close of US$0.7823/28.
It had bounced as far as US$0.7832 at one stage after Japanese buying emerged, supposedly related to the launch of a 30 billion yen dual currency saumurai bond for the European Investment Bank.
There was talk of more issues to come as the recent widening in the Australian yield spread over the U.S. had made the A$ attractive once more to Japanese retail investors.
However, the impact on the A$ was short lived as the yen benefited from a jump in Japanese yields and stock prices.
The yield on the key 10 year JGB leapt to 2.42 percent from 2.30 percent, partly in reaction to a whopping 666 point rise in the Nikkei share index to 20,181.

Analysts said a sustained recovery in stock prices promised to shore up Japanese bank balance sheets and reinforce the economic recovery there, which in turn raised the long-buried possibility of a tightening in monetary policy.

This was an untimely development for A$ bulls given all the talk of a domestic rate cut, and the currency bowed before the yen to 98.07/17 from an early 98.88/98 and 99.04/14 late Monday. It also dipped to 60.7 in trade weighted terms from 60.8.

Analysts think the chance of an RBA easing should be slim given leading indicators are pointing to a pick up in growth as the year progresses and the latest data on wages were a little higher than the central bank would have liked.

Nevertheless, the weakness of the labour market and a benign outlook for inflation meant an easing could not be entirely ruled out and traders expected the market to be tense ahead of the bank's 9.30 a.m. market operation on Wednesday -- the first opportunity for the RBA to announce any change.
If the bank stayed silent the market would normally assume policy was on hold but in this case there was a crucial caveat.
Namely that jobs data for April were due on Thursday. It was the falls in employment seen the two previous months which first stirred talk the RBA could ease again.

Most analysts were confident employment would bounce back in April, but warned it was impossible to rule out the risk of another drop, in which case the chance of an official easing would rise dramatically.

If one thing was certain, it was that the dollar had not discounted a cut and would drop like a stone if the cash rate fell another 0.5 point to 5.5 percent -- putting it in line with the Fed funds rate for the first time since the early 1980s.
A taste of the potential fallout came from New Zealand today as surprisingly weak jobs data greatly increased pressure for lower interest rates and sent the Kiwi tumbling.
The local dollar jumped to NZ$1.1360/76 as a result from an early NZ$1.1308/22.

Elsewhere, there was talk the government would confirm the he winning bids for three Federal airports on Wednesday which were expected to fetch up to A$3 billion. This could help support the dollar since the offshore members of the bidding groups may have a need to buy dollars.
